title: LQA-PROD-F: short_dialogue (noticeboard_lost_and_found)
topic: Two neighbors discuss how a new lost-and-found noticeboard near their building's mailboxes works.
transcript:
Dana: Have you seen the new board by the mailboxes?
Marcus: The wooden one with the little pins?
Dana: Yes, the building manager set it up last month for lost and found notices.
Marcus: I noticed someone posted about a missing set of keys.
Dana: Right, and there is also a section for items people found, like an umbrella and a child's glove.
Marcus: Does anyone actually check it?
Dana: Apparently people take photographs on their phones now instead of writing things down, so notices get answered faster.
Marcus: That is clever. I should post about the scarf I lost near the elevator.
Dana: Do it before someone else claims it as their own.
highlight_spans: set it up last month for lost and found notices
people take photographs on their phones now instead of writing things down, so notices get answered faster

questions.question_text: According to Dana, why do notices on the board get answered faster now?

options.text: Because the manager now checks the board every single morning.
options.explanation_he: אין אזכור בשיחה שהמנהל בודק את הלוח מדי בוקר; זהו פרט שלא נאמר.

options.text: Because people photograph notices with their phones and respond more quickly.
options.explanation_he: דנה אומרת במפורש שאנשים מצלמים את המודעות בטלפון במקום להעתיק אותן, ולכן התגובה מהירה יותר.

options.text: Because fewer people post notices than they did before.
options.explanation_he: זהו היפוך: השיחה לא אומרת שיש פחות מודעות, אלא שהתגובה עליהן מהירה יותר.

options.text: Because Marcus began writing replies directly on the board.
options.explanation_he: מרקוס הוא זה ששוקל לפרסם מודעה על צעיף אבוד; הוא לא מי שכתב תשובות על הלוח.

title: LQA-PROD-F: short_lecture (allotment_waiting_list)
topic: A narrator explains how a parish council manages and prunes its allotment garden waiting list.
transcript: Anyone wanting an allotment plot in this town must first join a waiting list managed by the parish council. Names are added in the order they apply, and plots become available only when a current gardener gives one up. Because demand rose sharply after gardening grew popular again, some applicants now wait more than three years before a plot opens. To keep the list current, the council sends a yearly letter asking whether people still want a place, and anyone who does not reply within a set period is removed. Officials say this yearly check has shortened the effective list considerably, since many names on it belonged to people who had already found space elsewhere.

the council sends a yearly letter asking whether people still want a place
this yearly check has shortened the effective list considerably

options.text: How gardeners are taught to grow vegetables more efficiently.
options.explanation_he: אין בהרצאה שום התייחסות להדרכת גננים בגידול ירקות; זהו פרט שלא נזכר כלל.

options.text: How the town manages and maintains its allotment waiting list.
options.explanation_he: כל ההרצאה מתארת כיצד נרשמים לרשימת ההמתנה וכיצד המועצה שומרת אותה מעודכנת מדי שנה.

title: LQA-PROD-F: short_dialogue (babysitting_co_op)
topic: Two neighbors discuss how a neighborhood babysitting point-exchange circle is organized.
transcript:
Priya: How does the babysitting circle actually work?
Owen: Parents earn points by watching other members' children, and they spend those points when they need a sitter themselves.
Priya: So no money changes hands at all?
Owen: None. The organizer just keeps a shared notebook that tracks everyone's balance.
Priya: What happens if someone runs out of points?
Owen: They can still request a sitter, but they go to the bottom of the list until their balance improves.
Priya: That seems fair. How do new families join?
Owen: They attend one meeting, agree to the rules, and start with a small number of points already in their account.
highlight_spans: Parents earn points by watching other members' children
they go to the bottom of the list until their balance improves

questions.question_text: According to Owen, what happens to a family whose point balance runs out?

options.text: They remain eligible for a sitter but are placed lower on the request list.
options.explanation_he: אוון אומר שהם עדיין יכולים לבקש שמרטפית, אבל הם עוברים לתחתית הרשימה עד שהיתרה שלהם משתפרת.

options.text: They must attend an extra meeting before requesting a sitter again.
options.explanation_he: אין אזכור בשיחה לפגישה נוספת שיש להשתתף בה; זהו פרט שהומצא.

options.text: They are moved to the top of the list so their balance can recover.
options.explanation_he: זהו היפוך: לפי השיחה הם עוברים לתחתית הרשימה, לא לראש הרשימה.

options.text: New families must wait until their balance improves before joining at all.
options.explanation_he: התיאור הזה מתאים למשפחות קיימות שאזל להן היתרה, לא למשפחות חדשות המצטרפות למעגל.

title: LQA-PROD-F: short_lecture (litter_pick_group)
topic: A narrator describes how a volunteer litter-picking group organizes its biweekly walks and record keeping.
transcript: Every second Saturday, a group of local volunteers meets outside the community center to clear litter from the riverside path and the park beyond it. The organizer divides the walkers into small teams, each assigned a different stretch so no area gets covered twice. Bags and gloves are supplied by the town council, though volunteers are encouraged to bring their own reusable gloves if they have them. After the walk, everyone gathers back at the center to weigh the collected bags together, and the total is recorded in a logbook kept since the group began. Members say watching the yearly totals slowly fall has been the most encouraging part of taking part.

title: LQA-PROD-F: short_dialogue (street_chess_table)
topic: Two neighbors discuss the informal coin system that decides turns at a public square's stone chess table.
transcript:
Theo: Why is there always a crowd around that stone chess table in the square?
Iris: People have played there since the town rebuilt the square decades ago, and it just became a habit.
Theo: Do you need to sign up to play?
Iris: Not exactly. Whoever wins stays at the board, and the next challenger simply places a coin on the edge to mark their turn.
Theo: So no one keeps a formal list?
Iris: No list, just the coins lined up. Regulars say the unspoken rule has never caused an argument.
Theo: That is surprising for something so informal.
Iris: People here take it seriously without needing rules written down.

options.text: She believes the coin system often leads to disagreements among players.
options.explanation_he: זהו היפוך: איריס אומרת שהכלל הבלתי כתוב מעולם לא גרם לוויכוח.

title: LQA-PROD-F: short_lecture (toy_library)
topic: A narrator explains how a toy library lends out toys and relies on volunteers to inspect and clean returns.
transcript: A toy library operates much like a book library, except the shelves hold puzzles, building blocks, and board games instead of novels. Families pay a small yearly membership fee, then borrow toys for a few weeks at a time before returning them and choosing something new. Volunteers inspect every returned item, checking that all the pieces are present and cleaning anything that needs it before the toy goes back on the shelf. Because toys rotate through so many households, organizers say children are exposed to a much wider variety of play than most families could otherwise afford. The library relies entirely on donated toys and a small team of volunteers to keep the shelves stocked and organized.

title: Resizing a Ring at the Jeweler's Bench
transcript:
Elena: To make this ring smaller, I cut through the band on one side with a fine saw blade, right where the join used to be.
Sam: So you're removing a piece of metal entirely?
Elena: Exactly. I measure how much needs to come out, cut that section free, and then bring the two open ends back together so they touch cleanly.
Sam: How do they stay together after that?
Elena: I heat the seam with a small torch and add a matching alloy that melts and flows into the gap, fusing the ends into one solid ring again.
Sam: Does the heating change the shape at all?
Elena: A little, so the last step is filing the seam smooth and rounding the band back on a steel mandrel until it sits evenly on your finger.
Sam: That sounds much more careful than I expected.
Elena: It has to be, otherwise the ring will read as thinner exactly where we joined it.

title: Rebacking a Book Spine at the Bindery
transcript:
Priya: This old spine has cracked away from the boards, so the first thing I do is lift the original leather carefully with a bone knife.
Tom: You don't throw the old spine away?
Priya: No, I save it, because once the book is repaired I'll paste that same piece back on top to keep the original look.
Tom: What happens underneath while it's off?
Priya: I clean out the old glue, then attach a strip of new material across the spine so it bridges the boards and the pages again.
Tom: Is that strip strong enough by itself?
Priya: It needs help, so I press it firmly and let it dry under weight overnight before touching the book again.
Tom: And that's when the old leather goes back on?
Priya: Right, I paste it down last, working it into the grooves so the repair barely shows and the spine flexes normally when you open the covers.

title: Truing a Bicycle Wheel
transcript:
Noah: Your wheel has a wobble, so I start by spinning it slowly in the stand and watching where the rim drifts sideways against this pointer.
Ivy: So you can see exactly where the bend is?
Noah: Yes, and once I find the loose section, I turn the spoke nipples there with this small wrench, tightening some and loosening others.
Ivy: How do you know which spokes to adjust?
Noah: The rim pulls toward whichever side has the tighter spokes, so I loosen that side slightly and tighten the opposite spokes to pull it back straight.
Ivy: Do you just do that once?
Noah: No, I spin it again after every small adjustment and keep repeating the process until the rim runs true and barely brushes the pointer.
Ivy: It looks like patient work.
Noah: It is, small turns matter more than big ones here.

title: The Routine at a Shoe-Shine Stand
transcript: At the shoe-shine stand on the corner, the routine always starts the same way. The shiner brushes off loose dust and dried mud with a stiff brush, working from the toe back toward the heel so grit does not get pressed into the leather. Next comes a thin layer of cream polish, rubbed in with a soft cloth in small circles until the color evens out across every scuff. The shiner lets that layer sit for a minute so the leather can absorb it fully before doing anything else. After that, a wax polish goes on in an even thinner coat, and this is buffed hard with a separate cloth, snapped tight between both hands, until the surface starts to catch the light. Some customers expect the whole process to take only a minute or two, yet a careful shiner spends closer to ten, since rushing the buffing stage leaves the wax looking cloudy instead of glossy.

title: Restringing a Tennis Racket
transcript: Restringing a tennis racket at the shop follows a simple sequence. First the old strings are cut out from the center, released gradually so the frame does not flex unevenly while tension drops on one side only. Once the frame is bare, a fresh piece of string is threaded through the main holes, running vertically from top to bottom, and each pass is pulled to the exact tension the player asked for on the machine. After the vertical strings are locked in place with small knots at the frame edge, the cross strings are woven over and under them, one at a time, starting from the throat of the racket and working up toward the top. Each cross string is also pulled to tension before being tied off. The final step is trimming the loose ends close to the knots so nothing catches on a player's fingers during a match.

title: Replacing a Spade Handle
transcript: Replacing a broken handle on a garden spade is mostly about removing the old wood cleanly. The repair starts with drilling out the rivets that hold the handle inside the metal collar, since prying the wood out with those still in place usually splits the collar. Once the rivets are gone, the cracked handle is knocked free with a mallet, leaving just the empty metal socket. A new handle, already shaped to match the socket, is tapped in from the top until it seats fully against the collar with no visible gap. Fresh holes are drilled through the collar and handle together so the new rivets line up exactly where the old ones sat. The rivets are hammered through and the ends filed flat. A quick wipe with an oiled cloth protects the fresh wood, and the tool is ready for the garden again, well before the end of the afternoon.

title: LQA-PROD-F: long_dialogue (millinery_hat_blocking)
topic: An apprentice milliner asks a senior milliner to explain the order of steps that turns steamed felt into a finished blocked hat.
transcript:
Priya: Owen, before I ruin another hood, can you explain how steamed felt becomes a finished hat?
Owen: Happy to. It starts with steaming. The felt hood goes over the kettle until the fibers soften enough to stretch without tearing.
Priya: So steaming has to come first, no matter what?
Owen: Right, because a stiff hood would crack the moment you pulled it down over the crown block. Once it softens, you ease it over the block by hand, working outward from the center until the dome sits flush.
Priya: And the brim comes after the crown is set?
Owen: It does. Because the crown has already taken its shape on the block, the loose felt hanging below it can be pulled flat and worked over the brim block without dragging the dome out of shape.
Priya: However, doesn't the brim just flop back once you let go of it?
Owen: It would, which is why the blocking cord goes on next. You tie it tightly around the base of the crown, right where the brim meets it, and that tension holds the brim's angle while everything dries.
Priya: So the cord is doing more work than I assumed.
Owen: Much more. People assume the crown block alone fixes the shape, but the block only holds the dome; it's really the cord's tension that locks the brim's angle in place. Without it, the felt would slowly relax back toward flat.
Priya: Yet the cord stays on for the entire drying time?
Owen: For hours, yes. Only once the felt is fully dry and rigid do we cut the cord away and move to pouncing, sanding the nap lightly so the surface looks even.
Priya: I always assumed pouncing came before blocking.
Owen: A common mix-up. Pouncing is strictly the final stage, done only after the shape has already become permanent.

questions.question_text: According to Owen, why must the felt be steamed before it goes over the crown block?

options.text: Because unsoftened felt cracks when stretched over the block
options.explanation_he: אווין אומר במפורש שכובע קשה היה נסדק ברגע שמותחים אותו מעל בלוק הכתר, ולכן חובה לרכך קודם באדים.

options.text: Because the brim block cannot shape unsteamed felt properly
options.explanation_he: זו הטענה הנכונה לגבי בלוק הכתר, אך היא מיוחסת כאן בטעות לבלוק השוליים, שמופיע רק בשלב מאוחר יותר.

options.text: Because the crown is blocked before any steaming starts
options.explanation_he: זהו היפוך סדר הפעולות: לפי השיחה האידוי קודם לעיצוב הכתר, לא להפך.

options.text: Because steaming removes natural oils before dyeing begins
options.explanation_he: אין בשיחה כל אזכור של הסרת שמנים או צביעה; זהו פרט מומצא שנשמע סביר אך אינו נתמך.

questions.question_text: What is the main point Owen makes about what actually holds the brim's angle in place?

options.text: The crown block's tight fit keeps the brim from moving
options.explanation_he: זוהי טענה מתחרה סבירה, אך אווין אומר במפורש שהבלוק רק מחזיק את הכיפה, לא את זווית השוליים.

options.text: The cord's tension while drying is what fixes the brim's angle
options.explanation_he: זהו הרעיון המרכזי שאווין מדגיש: המתח של החוט בזמן הייבוש הוא שקובע את זווית השוליים, לא הבלוק.

options.text: Pouncing smooths the surface enough to stop the brim sagging
options.explanation_he: פאונסינג מוזכר רק כשלב סופי של החלקת המשטח, ולא כמה שקובע את זווית השוליים.

options.text: Steaming softens felt permanently so it never relaxes back to flat
options.explanation_he: האידוי הוא רק ריכוך זמני; השיחה אומרת שבלי החוט הלבד היה נרגע בחזרה לשטוח, בניגוד לטענה כאן.

title: LQA-PROD-F: long_dialogue (silversmithing)
topic: An apprentice silversmith asks a master to explain the sequence of raising, annealing, planishing, and chasing that turns a flat disc into a finished bowl.
transcript:
Mara: Devon, could you walk me through how a flat silver disc actually turns into a bowl? I never follow the order.
Devon: Sure. It begins with raising. You hammer the flat disc over a stake in circles, moving the metal upward and inward until it starts to curve into a rough bowl shape.
Mara: And that's all done cold, straight through?
Devon: No, that's the trouble. Hammering work-hardens the silver, so after a few circuits the metal turns stiff and would split if you kept going. That's why annealing comes next: you heat the bowl until it glows dull red, then quench it, and the metal softens again.
Mara: So raising and annealing just alternate back and forth?
Devon: Exactly, several times, until the rough shape is deep enough. Once the form is close to finished, planishing takes over. You switch to a smooth, polished hammer and tap the whole surface in overlapping rows to erase the raising marks and true up the curve.
Mara: However, doesn't hammering that much just leave more dents in the metal?
Devon: It would with the wrong hammer, but a planishing hammer has no sharp edge, so each blow flattens rather than gouges. People assume raising alone gives a bowl its final smooth surface, but it's really the planishing stage that removes the ridges and leaves the metal even and reflective.
Mara: And chasing is separate from all of that work?
Devon: Completely separate. Chasing is decorative work done afterward, pushing patterns into the surface from the front with small punches, once the bowl's shape and finish are already settled.
Mara: Yet I've seen chasing tools that look almost like planishing hammers.
Devon: They're shaped differently once you look closely. Chasing punches are narrow and pointed, built for fine detail, not for shaping the whole bowl at once.

questions.question_text: According to Devon, which of the following is NOT true about raising?

options.text: It is done by hammering the disc over a stake
options.explanation_he: זהו פרט נכון: דבון אומר שהרייזינג נעשה בהלמת הדיסק מעל עמוד ברזל.

options.text: It gradually curves the metal upward and inward
options.explanation_he: זהו פרט נכון: המתכת זזה כלפי מעלה ופנימה עד שנוצרת צורת קערה גסה.

options.text: It uses a hammer with no sharp edge to prevent dents
options.explanation_he: זהו פרט שגוי המיוחס בטעות לרייזינג; זו למעשה תכונת הפטיש בשלב הפלנישינג, לא ברייזינג.

options.text: It must alternate with annealing to continue safely
options.explanation_he: זהו פרט נכון: המתכת מתקשה מההלמה ולכן צריך להחליף בין רייזינג לחישול שוב ושוב.

questions.question_text: What is the main point Devon makes about what actually gives a raised bowl its smooth, finished surface?

options.text: Raising alone smooths the surface once the shape is deep enough
options.explanation_he: טענה מתחרה סבירה, אך דבון אומר במפורש שאנשים טועים לחשוב כך; ההחלקה בפועל מגיעה מהפלנישינג.

options.text: Annealing removes the hammer marks left behind by raising
options.explanation_he: החישול רק מרכך את המתכת שוב; הסרת סימני ההלמה מיוחסת בטעות לחישול במקום לפלנישינג.

options.text: Chasing punches flatten the ridges before any polishing begins
options.explanation_he: צ'ייסינג הוא עבודה דקורטיבית שמתרחשת רק אחרי שהצורה והגימור כבר קבועים; אין קשר להחלקת הבליטות.

options.text: Planishing with a smooth hammer removes the ridges and evens the surface
options.explanation_he: זהו הרעיון המרכזי שדבון מדגיש: הפלנישינג עם הפטיש החלק הוא שמסיר את הבליטות ומחליק את המשטח.

title: LQA-PROD-F: long_dialogue (whisky_distilling)
topic: An apprentice asks a master distiller to explain the chain from mashing and fermentation through the wash still and spirit still to maturation.
transcript:
Fiona: Callum, can you explain how barley becomes whisky? I only know it involves stills somewhere.
Callum: Gladly. It starts with mashing. Crushed malted barley is mixed with hot water in the mash tun, and the heat releases sugars from the grain into a sweet liquid called wort.
Fiona: So the sugar has to come out before anything else can happen?
Callum: Exactly, because fermentation depends on it. Once the wort cools, yeast is added, and it feeds on those sugars, producing alcohol and carbon dioxide. Without the sugar from mashing, the yeast would have nothing to work on.
Fiona: And that fermented liquid goes straight to the still?
Callum: To the wash still first. It's the larger of the two, and it boils off a rough, weak spirit from the fermented wash. However, that first pass alone isn't strong enough to bottle.
Fiona: So it has to be distilled again?
Callum: Right, in the spirit still. That second, smaller still separates the batch into early, middle, and late portions of the run, keeping only the clean middle cut and discarding the rest.
Fiona: I assumed the wash still did that separating.
Callum: A common assumption, but no. It's the spirit still, and specifically that middle cut, that actually determines the flavor and safety of what ends up in the cask; the wash still just concentrates the alcohol.
Fiona: Yet the spirit isn't finished even after the cut?
Callum: Not close. It goes into oak casks for maturation, sometimes for many years, where the wood slowly shapes its color and flavor before it's ever called whisky.
Fiona: So maturation is the longest stage in the whole chain?
Callum: By far. Mashing, fermentation, and the two stills can all finish within a single week, but maturation alone can stretch on for a decade before the spirit is finally ready.

questions.question_text: According to the conversation, who initially assumed the wash still was responsible for separating the cut?

options.text: Fiona, before Callum explained the actual process to her
options.explanation_he: פיונה אומרת במפורש 'I assumed the wash still did that separating', וקאלום מתקן אותה.

options.text: Callum, before Fiona corrected his description of the stills
options.explanation_he: זהו היפוך תפקידים: קאלום הוא זה שמסביר ומתקן, לא פיונה שמתקנת אותו.

options.text: A visiting cooper touring the distillery with Fiona
options.explanation_he: אין בשיחה כל אזכור של חבתן מבקר; זהו פרט מומצא שאינו נתמך בתמליל.

options.text: Fiona, while asking about the mash tun's sugar extraction
options.explanation_he: ההנחה השגויה של פיונה נאמרה בהקשר לעמדות הזיקוק, לא בהקשר לגיגית המיצוי (mash tun).

questions.question_text: What is the main point Callum makes about what actually determines a whisky's flavor and safety?

options.text: The wash still's rough spirit already sets the whisky's final flavor
options.explanation_he: טענה מתחרה סבירה, אך קאלום אומר שהעמדה הראשונה מייצרת רק רוח גולמית וחלשה, לא את הטעם הסופי.

options.text: The middle cut taken in the spirit still determines the flavor and safety
options.explanation_he: זהו הרעיון המרכזי: קאלום אומר במפורש שדווקא החתך האמצעי בעמדת הרוח הוא שקובע טעם ובטיחות.

options.text: Maturation in oak casks is what determines the spirit's safety
options.explanation_he: ההבשלה מעצבת צבע וטעם לאורך זמן, אך הבטיחות מיוחסת בשיחה לבחירת החתך, לא להבשלה.

options.text: Fermentation length is what determines how safe the final spirit is
options.explanation_he: אורך התסיסה אינו מוזכר כלל כגורם בטיחות; זהו פרט מומצא שלא נתמך בתמליל.

highlight_spans: Without the sugar from mashing, the yeast would have nothing to work on
It's the spirit still, and specifically that middle cut, that actually determines the flavor and safety of what ends up in the cask

title: LQA-PROD-F: long_lecture (tanning_leatherworking)
topic: A lecture explaining how a hide moves through the beamhouse, liming, the tanning pit, and currying on its way to becoming finished leather.
transcript: Long before a hide becomes usable leather, it passes through the beamhouse, the first stage of a tannery. There, workers scrape away hair and flesh from the raw skin, using a curved blade drawn across a wooden beam. This cleaning has to happen before any tanning chemical will penetrate the hide evenly. Once the beamhouse work is finished, the hide moves into liming, where it soaks for days in a solution that loosens any remaining hair follicles and swells the fibers, opening the skin's structure so that tanning agents can later soak in fully. However, liming alone does not turn a hide into leather; it only prepares the fibers to accept treatment. The hide is then rinsed and lowered into the tanning pit, a deep vat where it rests among layers of ground tree bark for weeks or even months. It is this slow soak in the tanning pit, not the earlier liming, that actually converts the raw, rotting protein of the skin into a stable material that resists decay. Many assume the beamhouse does the real transformation, since that is where the hide first starts to look clean, but the pit is where the chemistry that defines leather actually happens. Yet even a fully tanned hide is still stiff and dull when it comes out of the pit. That is what currying corrects: skilled workers work oils and greases into the leather by hand, softening it and giving it the flexible, even finish that makes it usable for saddles, boots, or bookbindings. Without currying, tanned leather would remain too rigid for most everyday purposes.

questions.question_text: In this lecture, what does the word "swells" most nearly mean when describing what happens to the fibers during liming?

options.text: Makes them shrink tightly together
options.explanation_he: התמליל לא מתאר התכווצות; הליים מתואר כפותח את מבנה הסיבים, לא מכווץ אותו.

options.text: Makes them harden and resist tanning agents
options.explanation_he: זהו היפוך המשמעות: הליים דווקא פותח את הסיבים כדי שחומרי העיבוד יחדרו, לא סוגר עליהם.

options.text: Makes them expand and open up
options.explanation_he: בהקשר, 'swells' מתאר את הסיבים שמתרחבים ונפתחים, מה שמאפשר לחומרי העיבוד לחדור מאוחר יותר.

options.text: Makes them absorb bark tannins from the pit
options.explanation_he: ספיגת שברי הקליפה מתרחשת בשלב מאוחר יותר בבור השיזוף, לא במהלך שלב הליים עצמו.

questions.question_text: What is the main point this lecture makes about which stage actually turns a hide into leather?

options.text: The beamhouse is what truly transforms the raw hide
options.explanation_he: טענה מתחרה סבירה, שכן שם העור נראה נקי לראשונה, אך התמליל אומר במפורש שזו טעות נפוצה.

options.text: Currying is what gives the hide its final softness and flexibility
options.explanation_he: קארינג מתואר כשלב שמרכך ומגמר עור שכבר עבר שיזוף; ההמרה הכימית עצמה מיוחסת לבור השיזוף.

options.text: Liming alone chemically converts hide into finished leather
options.explanation_he: התמליל אומר במפורש שהליים רק מכין את הסיבים ואינו הופך את העור לעור מעובד בעצמו.

options.text: The tanning pit is what actually converts hide into stable leather
options.explanation_he: זהו הרעיון המרכזי: התמליל קובע שדווקא ההשריה הממושכת בבור השיזוף, לא הליים, היא שהופכת את העור ליציב.

highlight_spans: swells the fibers, opening the skin's structure so that tanning agents can later soak in fully
It is this slow soak in the tanning pit, not the earlier liming, that actually converts the raw, rotting protein of the skin into a stable material that resists decay

title: LQA-PROD-F: long_lecture (wood_turning_lathe)
topic: A lecture explaining how a block of wood moves through roughing, spindle turning, faceplate mounting, and parting on a lathe.
transcript: A block of wood destined for the lathe begins its transformation with the roughing gouge, a heavy, curved tool used to knock the corners off a square blank and turn it into a rough cylinder as it spins. This first pass removes the most material and is deliberately crude; accuracy comes later. Once the blank is round, the turner shifts to spindle turning, shaping the cylinder between the two centers of the lathe into the curves, beads, and coves that give a chair leg or a candlestick its final profile. However, not every piece is held between centers. Bowls and platters are mounted differently, screwed onto a faceplate at one end only, which lets the turner hollow out the inside face without the second center getting in the way. It is this switch to faceplate mounting, more than any single tool, that actually makes bowl turning possible, since a spindle held at both ends could never be hollowed out from the open face. Many beginners assume the roughing gouge does most of the shaping work throughout a project, but once the rough cylinder exists, the finer tools take over almost entirely. Yet even after the shape is finished, the piece is still attached to the lathe. That is where the parting tool comes in: a narrow blade that cuts straight inward to separate the finished piece cleanly from the waste wood still gripped by the chuck.

questions.question_text: According to the lecture, why is the first pass with the roughing gouge deliberately crude?

options.text: Because its only job is removing material and rough shaping
options.explanation_he: התמליל אומר במפורש שהמעבר הראשון מסיר הכי הרבה חומר ומכוון להיות גס בכוונה; הדיוק מגיע רק אחר כך.

options.text: Because spindle turning needs an imprecise starting shape
options.explanation_he: עיבוד הציר (spindle turning) הוא שלב הדיוק שמגיע אחרי הגלנדר הגס, ולא הסיבה לגסותו.

options.text: Because accuracy must come before the corners are removed
options.explanation_he: זהו היפוך הסדר: לפי התמליל הסרת הפינות קודמת לדיוק, לא להפך.

options.text: Because the wood must cool before finer cuts are safe
options.explanation_he: אין בתמליל כל אזכור של קירור העץ; זהו פרט מומצא שנשמע סביר אך אינו נתמך.

questions.question_text: What is the main point this lecture makes about what actually makes bowl turning possible?

options.text: The roughing gouge alone makes bowl turning possible from the very first cut
options.explanation_he: טענה מתחרה סבירה, אך התמליל אומר שהגלנדר הגס רק מסיר חומר בהתחלה, לא מה שמאפשר עיבוד קערות.

options.text: Mounting the wood on a faceplate is what makes bowl turning possible
options.explanation_he: זהו הרעיון המרכזי: התמליל קובע שהמעבר להרכבה על לוח החזית הוא מה שמאפשר לחלל את הקערה מהצד הפתוח.

options.text: The parting tool is what allows a bowl to be hollowed out

title: LQA-PROD-F: long_lecture (stone_quarrying_masonry)
topic: A lecture explaining how a quarried stone moves through plug-and-feather splitting, dressing on the banker, and coursing on its way into a finished wall.
transcript: Getting a usable block of stone out of a quarry face starts with plug-and-feather splitting. Workers drill a line of shallow holes along the stone, insert two curved metal feathers into each hole, then drive a steel plug between them with a hammer, one hole at a time, until the stress finally runs a clean crack the whole length of the line. This method lets quarrymen free a block without the shattering that blasting would cause. Once a rough block is free, it goes to the banker, the mason's sturdy bench, where dressing begins: a mason squares the block's faces with a chisel and mallet, working off the quarry marks left by the split. However, dressing alone does not make a wall; a beautifully squared block still has to fit against its neighbors. That fit depends on coursing, the practice of laying dressed stones in level, continuous rows so that the joints between one course align cleanly with the row above and below. It is coursing, not the dressing itself, that actually determines whether a wall stays strong under load, since poorly aligned joints concentrate weight onto single points rather than spreading it evenly across the row. Many people assume that fine dressing work is what gives a stone wall its strength, but even roughly dressed stone holds up well if the coursing is done correctly. Yet coursing decisions are made well before the mortar ever goes in, while the mason is still setting each stone dry to check the fit.

questions.question_text: According to the lecture, which of the following is NOT true about plug-and-feather splitting?

options.text: A neat row of evenly spaced holes is bored along the stone's face
options.explanation_he: זהו פרט נכון: התמליל מתאר קידוח שורה של חורים לאורך האבן.

options.text: Metal feathers are inserted before the plug is driven in
options.explanation_he: זהו פרט נכון: הנוצות המתכתיות מוכנסות לפני שהיתד מוכנס ונחבט בפטיש.

options.text: The stone is squared on the banker before any holes are drilled
options.explanation_he: זהו פרט שגוי: ריבוע האבן על הספסל (הבנקר) קורה בשלב הדרסינג, אחרי הבקיעה, לא לפניה.

options.text: A steel plug is driven between the feathers with a hammer
options.explanation_he: זהו פרט נכון: התמליל מתאר במפורש הכאת יתד פלדה בין הנוצות בעזרת פטיש.

questions.question_text: What is the main point this lecture makes about what actually determines a stone wall's strength?

options.text: Fine dressing work is what determines a stone wall's strength
options.explanation_he: טענה מתחרה סבירה, אך התמליל אומר במפורש שזו הנחה שגויה נפוצה; אפילו אבן גסה מחזיקה אם הקורסינג נכון.

options.text: Plug-and-feather splitting determines how strong the finished wall becomes
options.explanation_he: שיטת הבקיעה קובעת רק איך משחררים בלוק מהמחצבה; החוזק הסופי מיוחס בתמליל לקורסינג, לא לבקיעה.

options.text: The mortar added after coursing is what gives a wall its strength
options.explanation_he: התמליל אומר שהחלטות הקורסינג נעשות עוד לפני שהמלט נכנס כלל; אין תמיכה לטענה שהמלט הוא מקור החוזק.

options.text: Coursing, the alignment of the stones, is what determines a wall's strength
options.explanation_he: זהו הרעיון המרכזי: התמליל קובע שדווקא הקורסינג, לא הדרסינג עצמו, הוא שקובע אם הקיר יישאר חזק תחת עומס.
